Silicosis among stone quarry workers is documented across Rajasthan, Madhya
Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and the diagnosis is consistently late because
screening camps are rare and irregular in the districts where the quarries
operate.

The affected-led response is a workers' association that files compensation
claims and tracks deaths the state registry does not count, and it operates
with almost no institutional funding of its own, relying instead on a small
number of individual donors and occasional grants that rarely survive past a
single cycle.

Government compensation schemes exist on paper in every state with active
quarrying, and every one of them requires a certified diagnosis from a
government hospital before a claim can be filed, and every one of those
hospitals is hours away from the quarries by road, and the certifying doctors
rotate through the post so quickly that continuity of care for a single
worker across the years a silicosis diagnosis actually takes to confirm is
essentially impossible, and so the paper scheme and the lived reality of a
quarry worker's actual path to a diagnosis and a payout diverge sharply, with
the gap between the two absorbing years of a worker's remaining working life
before any claim is even filed, let alone paid, and this is true whether the
worker is in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat or any of the
other states where the same instrument -- a certified-diagnosis requirement
routed through a hospital system that does not reach the quarries -- recurs
in the same shape, decade after decade, without the underlying mismatch
between where the authority to certify sits and where the harm is actually
occurring ever being closed by any of the states running the scheme, which
is itself a textbook instance of authority mismatched to harm rather than a
one-off administrative failure limited to a single state's implementation,
and the same pattern recurs in every neighbouring sector that routes a
diagnosis-gated benefit through a facility the intended beneficiary cannot
reasonably reach, from black lung compensation in coal-belt districts to
pesticide-poisoning claims in cotton-growing regions, none of which have
ever closed the distance between the certifying authority's location and
the working population's actual geography, decade after decade, budget
cycle after budget cycle, ministry after ministry, regardless of which
political party held office in the state capital at the time, and none of
the reform proposals that have been floated over that period, whether
mobile certification vans, telemedicine pilots, or block-level camps, has
survived past a single funding cycle long enough to be evaluated on
whether it actually closed the gap it was designed to close, which is
itself a recurring feature of how this particular mismatch gets addressed
on paper without ever being addressed in the district where the harm is
actually occurring.

सिलिकोसिस पीड़ित संघ has documented cases the state registry does not carry,
and दिनेश रायसिंह has spoken publicly about the certification bottleneck at
several state-level hearings on the subject over the last several years.
